claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative EMSA data measuring binding affinity.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 1-106 binds to all five types of nucleic acids (ssRNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, dsDNA, RNA/DNA hybrids) with similar affinities.
claims.source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound to all five types of nucleic acids with similar affinities, ranging from 61 ± 5 nM for ssRNA to 185 ± 17 nM for dsDNA (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by EMSA data testing different nucleic acid types.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 1-106 bound α-satellite RNA with a dissociation constant of 23 ± 2 nM.
claims.source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound α-satellite or β-actin RNA with similar affinities: 23 ± 2 nM and 32 ± 2 nM, respectively (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by EMSA data measuring binding to α-satellite RNA.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 1-106 bound β-actin RNA with a dissociation constant of 32 ± 2 nM.
claims.source: We found that SUV39H1 1–106 bound α-satellite or β-actin RNA with similar affinities: 23 ± 2 nM and 32 ± 2 nM, respectively (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by EMSA data measuring binding to β-actin RNA.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids with minimal sequence preference.
claims.source: We conclude that SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids, has minimal sequence preference for the sequences tested thus far, and that binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Inferred from EMSA data showing similar binding to different sequences and nucleic acid types.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length.
claims.source: We conclude that SUV39H1 can bind both double- and single-stranded nucleic acids, has minimal sequence preference for the sequences tested thus far, and that binding affinity increases with increasing nucleic acid length (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by EMSA data comparing binding to 19mer, 50mer, and 180mer nucleic acids.

claims.claim: The R55A and R84A mutations almost completely abolished RNA binding by SUV39H1.
claims.source: By performing a more comprehensive analysis of the binding of these 23 mutants (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), we discovered two mutations, R55A and R84A, that almost completely abolished RNA binding by SUV39H1, reducing the affinity over 40-fold compared to WT (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by EMSA and filter binding assay data comparing mutant and WT SUV39H1.

claims.claim: Neither SUV39H1R55A nor SUV39H1R84A alter the binding of SUV39H1 to H3K9me3.
claims.source: Importantly, neither of the nucleic acid binding mutants (SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A) alter the binding of SUV39H1 to H3K9me3 (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by peptide binding assay data showing no change in H3K9me3 binding for these mutants.

claims.claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A completely disrupts binding to H3K9me3.
claims.source: As previously reported, we found that the WT SUV39H1 chromodomain preferentially binds to H3K9me3 compared to H3K9me0, and this binding is completely disrupted by the aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A (Figure 4E and F) (Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by peptide binding assay data and cited previous findings.

claims.claim: The R55A, R84A, and F43A mutations had no effect on the methyltransferase activity of full-length SUV39H1.
claims.source: We also confirmed that the R55A, R84A, and F43A mutations had no effect on the methyltransferase activity of full-length SUV39H1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: Supported by histone methyltransferase assay data.

claims.claim: The addition of RNA inhibits SUV39H1 methyltransferase activity.
claims.source: Interestingly, the addition of RNA inhibits SUV39H1 activity, as has been previously shown for PRC2 and several other SET domain histone methyltransferases (Cifuentes-Rojas et al., 2014; Kaneko et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by histone methyltransferase assay data and cited previous findings.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 colocalizes with EU-labeled RNA at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: In SUV39H1-GFP expressing HeLa cells, SUV39H1 colocalizes with EU-labeled RNA at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing colocalization.

claims.claim: α-satellite RNA was enriched 13 ± 2 fold in the WT SUV39H1 IP compared to GFP alone.
claims.source: We found that α-satellite RNA was enriched in the WT SUV39H1 IP 13 ± 2 fold when compared to GFP alone (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and that R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA to 45 ± 16% of the levels bound to WT (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-qPCR data.

claims.claim: The R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA bound to SUV39H1 to 45 ± 16% of WT levels.
claims.source: We found that α-satellite RNA was enriched in the WT SUV39H1 IP 13 ± 2 fold when compared to GFP alone (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and that R55A mutation reduced the amount of α-satellite RNA to 45 ± 16% of the levels bound to WT (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA immunoprecipitation and RT-qPCR data.

claims.claim: The R55A mutation did not disrupt SUV39H1's association with HP1α.
claims.source: In addition, the R55A mutation did not disrupt SUV39H1's association with HP1α, indicating that α-satellite RNA binding to SUV39H1 is not occurring indirectly through HP1α (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing HP1α binding to SUV39H1R55A.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 associates with α-satellite RNA in cells.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that SUV39H1 associates with α-satellite RNA in cells, and that this association is facilitated by the nucleic acid binding activity of the SUV39H1 chromodomain.
claims.evidence: Inferred from RNA immunoprecipitation data showing enrichment of α-satellite RNA with SUV39H1.

claims.claim: The R55A and R84A nucleic acid binding mutants of SUV39H1 showed defects in localization, reducing SUV39H1 signal to about half of WT levels.
claims.source: The R55A and R84A nucleic acid binding mutants of SUV39H1 showed defects in localization, reducing SUV39H1 signal by about half (R55A: 42 ± 8% of WT levels, R84A: 45 ± 9% of WT levels) (Figure 6A, B and C); indicating that the direct interaction of SUV39H1 with nucleic acids is important for its localization to pericentric heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: The aromatic cage mutants W64A and F43A led to more pronounced localization defects than the nucleic acid binding mutants.
claims.source: We also found that the aromatic cage mutants W64A and F43A led to more pronounced localization defects than those caused by the nucleic acid binding mutants (W64A: 10 ± 4% of WT levels, F43A: 15 ± 5% of WT levels) (Figure 6A, B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: Both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding contribute to SUV39H1 localization to pericentric heterochromatin during mitosis.
claims.source: These results suggest that both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding contribute to SUV39H1 localization to pericentric heterochromatin during mitosis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from localization data comparing different SUV39H1 mutants.

claims.claim: RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of WT SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the undigested control.
claims.source: RNase A treatment reduced the pericentric localization of SUV39H1 to 43 ± 4% of the undigested control, similar to the levels of the untreated SUV39H1R55A mutant in the same experiments (52 ± 9% of WT) (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: RNase A treatment did not significantly reduce the amount of SUV39H1R55A at pericentric chromatin.
claims.source: This is further supported by the fact that RNase A treatment did not significantly reduce the amount of SUV39H1R55A at pericentric chromatin (untreated: 52 ± 9%, RNase A: 42 ± 5%) (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claims.claim: Direct binding to both chromosome-associated RNA and H3K9me2/3 are required for proper localization of SUV39H1 to pericentric heterochromatin.
claims.source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that direct binding to both chromosome-associated RNA and H3K9me2/3 are required for proper localization of SUV39H1 to pericentric heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: Inferred from combined data on RNase treatment and mutant localization.

claims.claim: HP1α localization at heterochromatin is sensitive to RNase treatment.
claims.source: Previous studies found that HP1α localization at heterochromatin is sensitive to RNase treatment in both mouse interphase cells and on human mitotic chromosomes (Maison et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2007). We also observed a reduction in HP1α levels on chromatin after RNase A treatment, to 77 ± 13% of control levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data and cited previous findings.

claims.claim: Expressing SUV39H1-GFP for 6 hours caused a 1.5-fold increase in HP1α localization.
claims.source: Consistent with this, expressing SUV39H1-GFP for 6 hr, which causes an increase in SUV39H1-GFP at pericentric regions, also caused a 1.5-fold increase in HP1α localization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), in the absence of any detectable change in H3K9me3 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: RNase A treatment abolished the increase in HP1α localization following exogenous SUV39H1-GFP expression.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed that RNase A treatment abolished the increase in HP1α localization following exogenous SUV39H1-GFP expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: The extent of HP1α localization positively correlated with SUV39H1 localization after expressing SUV39H1 mutants.
claims.source: Finally, after expressing SUV39H1 mutants, the extent of HP1α localization positively correlated with SUV39H1 localization (Figure 6A and C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data comparing different mutants.

claims.claim: WT SUV39H1 recovered with an average half-time of 27 ± 7 s in FRAP experiments.
claims.source: After photobleaching, WT SUV39H1 recovered with an average half-time of 27 ± 7 s (Figure 7D), with a stable, immobile fraction of SUV39H1 that did not recover during the time frame of our experiment (Figure 7B, C and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: The mobile fraction of WT SUV39H1 represented 58 ± 7% of the total nuclear SUV39H1.
claims.source: The mobile fraction represented 58 ± 7% of the total nuclear SUV39H1 (Figure 7E), consistent with previous measurements (Hahn et al., 2013; Krouwels et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data and cited previous findings.

claims.claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1W64A had a recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 s.
claims.source: The aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7C), which disrupt binding to H3K9me3, had a much faster recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 and 5 ± 1 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: The aromatic cage mutant SUV39H1F43A had a recovery half-time of 5 ± 1 s.
claims.source: The aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7C), which disrupt binding to H3K9me3, had a much faster recovery half-time of 6 ± 2 and 5 ± 1 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: Approximately 90-95% of each aromatic cage mutant (W64A and F43A) was determined to be mobile within the nucleus.
claims.source: Unlike WT SUV39H1, approximately 90–95% of each aromatic cage mutant was determined to be mobile within the nucleus (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: The nucleic acid binding deficient mutant SUV39H1R55A showed an average recovery time of 14 ± 3 s.
claims.source: Interestingly, the nucleic acid binding deficient mutants SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1R84A (Figure 7C) showed an average recovery time in between that of WT SUV39H1 and the H3K9me3 binding mutants, with half-lives of 14 ± 3 and 13 ± 2 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: The nucleic acid binding deficient mutant SUV39H1R84A showed an average recovery time of 13 ± 2 s.
claims.source: Interestingly, the nucleic acid binding deficient mutants SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7B) and SUV39H1R84A (Figure 7C) showed an average recovery time in between that of WT SUV39H1 and the H3K9me3 binding mutants, with half-lives of 14 ± 3 and 13 ± 2 s, respectively (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: Both SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A demonstrated a level of mobility (77% ± 6) that was greater than WT SUV39H1, but less than the aromatic cage mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with this trend, both SUV39H1R55A and SUV39H1R84A demonstrated a level of mobility (77% ± 6) that was greater than WT SUV39H1, but less than the aromatic cage mutants SUV39H1W64A and SUV39H1F43A (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data.

claims.claim: Direct binding to nucleic acids stabilizes the association of SUV39H1 with chromatin in interphase cells.
claims.source: Combined with our in vitro biochemical analysis, these observations support a model in which direct binding to nucleic acids stabilizes the association of SUV39H1 with chromatin in interphase cells as well as in mitosis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from FRAP data showing intermediate recovery kinetics for nucleic acid binding mutants.

claims.claim: The RNA Pol I inhibitor CX-5461 decreased the fluorescence recovery half-time of WT SUV39H1 from 27 ± 7 s to 16 ± 3 s.
claims.source: When we added the RNA Pol I inhibitor CX-5461 – a treatment that we saw reduces RNA localization on mitotic chromosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) – the fluorescence recovery half-time of WT SUV39H1 decreased from 27 ± 7 s to 16 ± 3 s, comparable to the half-time of the nucleic acid binding mutant SUV39H1R55A (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data with RNA polymerase inhibitor treatment.

claims.claim: Total H3K9me3 levels were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants (R55A, F43A, R55A/F43A) compared to WT SUV39H1.
claims.source: We found that total H3K9me3 levels, as well as H3K9me3 localization at centromeres, were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants compared to WT SUV39H1 (Figure 8B, C, D and E), demonstrating a role for both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding by SUV39H1 in maintaining normal H3K9 methylation levels.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 localization at centromeres was reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants (R55A, F43A, R55A/F43A) compared to WT SUV39H1.
claims.source: We found that total H3K9me3 levels, as well as H3K9me3 localization at centromeres, were reduced in all SUV39H1 mutants compared to WT SUV39H1 (Figure 8B, C, D and E), demonstrating a role for both H3K9me3 binding and nucleic acid binding by SUV39H1 in maintaining normal H3K9 methylation levels.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claims.claim: α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold in the R55A mutant cell line compared to WT.
claims.source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claims.claim: α-satellite expression increased 1.56-fold in the F43A mutant cell line compared to WT.
claims.source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claims.claim: α-satellite expression increased 2.10-fold in the R55A/F43A double mutant cell line compared to WT.
claims.source: We found that α-satellite expression increased 1.35-fold, 1.56-fold, and 2.10-fold, in the R55A, F43A, and the R55A/F43A double mutant cells lines, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from endogenous SUV39H1 mutant cell lines.

claims.claim: A significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A.
claims.source: Interestingly, although no change in H3K9me3 was detected between the F43A single mutant and the R55A/F43A double mutant (Figure 8C and D), a significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A (Figure 8F), indicating that SUV39H1 nucleic binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data comparing F43A and R55A/F43A mutants.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 nucleic acid binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
claims.source: Interestingly, although no change in H3K9me3 was detected between the F43A single mutant and the R55A/F43A double mutant (Figure 8C and D), a significant increase in α-satellite RNA levels was observed in R55A/F43A compared to F43A (Figure 8F), indicating that SUV39H1 nucleic binding may make H3K9me3-independent contributions to heterochromatin function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of α-satellite RNA levels in F43A and R55A/F43A mutants despite similar H3K9me3 levels.

claims.claim: Both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding by SUV39H1 contribute to silencing of constitutive heterochromatin in human cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding by SUV39H1 contribute to silencing of constitutive heterochromatin in human cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from combined data showing increased α-satellite RNA expression in both nucleic acid binding and H3K9me3 binding mutants.

claims.claim: Chromatin-associated RNA contributes to the localization of SUV39H1 at constitutive heterochromatin in humans.
claims.source: In this study, we establish that chromatin-associated RNA contributes to the localization of SUV39H1 at constitutive heterochromatin in humans.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 binds without any observed sequence preference to both DNA and RNA in vitro.
claims.source: We show that SUV39H1 binds without any observed sequence preference to both DNA and RNA in vitro, and that SUV39H1 binds RNA transcribed from pericentromeric repeats in human cells.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on EMSA data showing similar binding to different sequences.

claims.claim: Mutations that disrupt the nucleic acid binding function of SUV39H1 cause defects in its localization to pericentric heterochromatin.
claims.source: Mutations that disrupt the nucleic acid binding function of SUV39H1 cause defects in its localization to pericentric heterochromatin, destabilize SUV39H1's association with chromatin, and result in heterochromatin silencing defects.
claims.evidence: Summary statement based on localization, FRAP, and silencing data from nucleic acid binding mutants.

claims.claim: The direct binding of SUV39H1 to RNA and to methylated histones ensures proper constitutive heterochromatin function in humans.
claims.source: We propose a model in which the direct binding of SUV39H1 to RNA and to methylated histones ensures proper constitutive heterochromatin function in humans.
claims.evidence: Proposed model based on combined experimental findings.

claims.claim: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3).
claims.source: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3), and these histone modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including the SUV39 enzymes themselves and the HP1 family of proteins (Al-Sady et al., 2013; Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Müller et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: H3K9me2/3 modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including SUV39 enzymes and HP1 family proteins.
claims.source: SUV39 proteins catalyze the di- and tri-methylation of lysine 9 of histone H3 (H3K9me2/3), and these histone modifications are bound by chromodomain-containing proteins, including the SUV39 enzymes themselves and the HP1 family of proteins (Al-Sady et al., 2013; Bannister et al., 2001; Lachner et al., 2001; Müller et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: HP1 protein binding to H3K9me2/3 chromatin drives chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression through oligomerization.
claims.source: HP1 protein binding to H3K9me2/3 chromatin is then thought to drive chromatin compaction and transcriptional repression through oligomerization (Canzio et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2004; Grewal and Jia, 2007).
claims.evidence: Established model supported by citations.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 and H3K9me3 are predominately associated with constitutive heterochromatin.
claims.source: SUV39H1 and H3K9me3 are predominately associated with constitutive heterochromatin, which represses 'selfish' genetic elements and repetitive DNA to promote genomic stability (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014; Peters et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation.
claims.source: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation (Bernard et al., 2001); and in mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer (Peters et al., 2001; Ting et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: In mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer.
claims.source: In fission yeast, disruption of pericentric heterochromatin causes chromosome cohesion defects and chromosome missegregation (Bernard et al., 2001); and in mammals, defective pericentric heterochromatin and aberrant transcription of pericentric repeats are associated with genomic instability and cancer (Peters et al., 2001; Ting et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SUV39H1 and SUV39H2 double knockout mice exhibit reduced embryonic viability, small stature, chromosome instability, increased risk of tumor formation, and male infertility.
claims.source: These defects in constitutive heterochromatin are most evident in SUV39H1 and SUV39H2 double knockout mice, which exhibit reduced embryonic viability, small stature, chromosome instability, an increased risk of tumor formation, and male infertility owing to defective spermatogenesis (Peters et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: In fission yeast, the localization of pericentric heterochromatin proteins, including Clr4, relies on the RNAi machinery.
claims.source: In fission yeast, the localization of pericentric heterochromatin proteins, including the SUV39 homolog Clr4, relies on the RNAi machinery (Bühler and Moazed, 2007; Grewal and Jia, 2007; Moazed, 2011), and RNAi has also been implicated in heterochromatin formation in other eukaryotic systems as well (Fukagawa et al., 2004; Pal-Bhadra et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: RNA is involved in targeting SUV39H1 to telomeres and to the Oct4 locus.
claims.source: Recent studies reported that RNA is involved in targeting SUV39H1 to telomeres and to the Oct4 locus (Porro et al., 2014; Scarola et al., 2015); however, it is unclear whether RNA plays a broader role in SUV39H1-dependent heterochromatin formation, and if direct RNA binding regulates the association of SUV39H1 with pericentric heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Chromodomain-containing proteins can act as RNA binding domains.
claims.source: This is consistent with previous findings that chromodomains can act as RNA binding domains (Akhtar et al., 2000), and that the telomeric TERRA RNA associates with SUV39H1 (Porro et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The chromodomains of HP1 proteins specifically recognize methylated H3K9 through three conserved aromatic residues called the 'aromatic cage'.
claims.source: The chromodomains of HP1 proteins specifically recognize methylated H3K9 through three conserved aromatic residues, called the 'aromatic cage' (Bannister et al., 2001; Jacobs and Khorasanizadeh, 2002; Lachner et al., 2001; Nielsen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The SUV39H1 chromodomain specifically binds to methylated H3K9 peptides via three aromatic cage residues.
claims.source: The SUV39H1 chromodomain also specifically binds to methylated H3K9 peptides, most likely via three similar aromatic cage residues (Figure 4B) (Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation and structural data.

claims.claim: Transcription is largely repressed in mitosis.
claims.source: Because transcription is largely repressed in mitosis (Gottesfeld and Forbes, 1997), RNAs bound to mitotic chromosomes may be more likely to play regulatory roles than RNAs associated with chromatin during interphase.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Transcription by RNA polymerase II can occur from the core centromere regions of human mitotic chromosomes.
claims.source: A previous study demonstrated that transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) can occur from the core centromere regions of human mitotic chromosomes (Chan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Direct RNA binding by PRC2 and HP1α is important for their proper localization and function.
claims.source: The finding that RNA is bound to the pericentric regions of human mitotic chromosomes is intriguing in light of previous observations that direct RNA binding by the heterochromatin factors Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) and HP1α is important for their proper localization and function (Muchardt et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Mouse HP1α protein can directly bind RNA.
claims.source: SUV39H1 binds directly to HP1 proteins (Yamamoto and Sonoda, 2003), and mouse HP1α protein can directly bind RNA (Muchardt et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The RNA-dependent mechanism for SUV39 function appears to be present in both human and mouse cells.
claims.source: Importantly, the RNA-dependent mechanism for SUV39 function appears to be present in both human and mouse cells (Shirai et al., 2017; Velazquez Camacho et al., 2017) suggesting a conserved role for RNA in regulating constitutive heterochromatin.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

results.result: α-satellite RNA localizes in cis at pericentric heterochromatin on human mitotic chromosomes. This RNA is enriched at pericentric regions in multiple cell lines (both primary and immortalized), colocalizes with H3K9me3 but not with the core centromere marker HEC1, and is sensitive to RNase A treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C8 provide converging evidence from EU-RNA labeling, RNA FISH with α-satellite probes, RNase sensitivity assays, and colocalization studies with heterochromatin markers. The data demonstrate that α-satellite RNA is specifically localized at pericentric regions where it is transcribed (in cis), supported by multiple experimental approaches and cell lines.

results.result: Pericentric RNA is primarily transcribed by RNA polymerase I within 4 hours before mitosis. Treatment with Pol I inhibitors (actinomycin D, CX-5461) completely eliminates pericentric RNA signal, while Pol II inhibitors only reduce it by ~50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 are supported by RNA polymerase inhibitor experiments and pulse-chase labeling studies. The differential sensitivity to Pol I vs. Pol II inhibitors and the timing data from EU pulse-chase experiments provide clear evidence for the transcriptional source and timing of pericentric RNA synthesis.

results.result: SUV39H1 localization to pericentric heterochromatin depends on the presence of RNA. RNase A treatment reduces SUV39H1 pericentric localization to 43% of control levels, and this effect can be rescued by RNase inhibitors, without affecting chromosome structure or total SUV39H1 protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 demonstrate RNA-dependent SUV39H1 localization through RNase treatment experiments with appropriate controls. The rescue with RNase inhibitors (C12), preservation of DNA staining (C13), and unchanged protein levels (C14) rule out non-specific effects and support the conclusion that RNA is required for SUV39H1 localization.

results.result: SUV39 DKO cells show reduced H3K9me3 and HP1α localization but increased α-satellite RNA levels, while α-satellite RNA continues to localize at pericentric regions. Global RNA expression levels remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 characterize the SUV39 DKO phenotype using western blotting, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, and RNA-seq. The data demonstrate that loss of SUV39 enzymes disrupts heterochromatin silencing (increased satellite RNA) and reduces H3K9me3/HP1α, but does not affect global transcription or the cis-localization of α-satellite RNA.

results.result: The chromodomain of SUV39H1 (residues 42-106) is sufficient for RNA binding activity with a Kd of 2.31 ± 0.17 µM. The N-terminal extension (residues 1-106) increases binding affinity 16-fold to a Kd of 0.15 ± 0.01 µM.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 are supported by systematic EMSA experiments with SUV39H1 truncations. The quantitative binding data clearly demonstrate that the chromodomain is sufficient for RNA binding and that the N-terminal extension enhances this activity, with well-defined dissociation constants.

results.result: SUV39H1 binds to multiple nucleic acid types (ssRNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, dsDNA, RNA/DNA hybrids) with similar affinities (61-185 nM) and shows minimal sequence preference. Binding affinity increases with nucleic acid length.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are supported by comprehensive EMSA experiments testing different nucleic acid types, sequences (α-satellite vs. β-actin), and lengths. The similar Kd values across different nucleic acid types and sequences support the conclusion of promiscuous, length-dependent binding with minimal sequence specificity.

results.result: The R55A and R84A mutations abolish RNA binding by SUV39H1 (>40-fold reduction in affinity) without affecting H3K9me3 binding or methyltransferase activity. The F43A aromatic cage mutant disrupts H3K9me3 binding but not methyltransferase activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 demonstrate successful separation of nucleic acid binding from H3K9me3 binding functions through mutagenesis. The data from EMSAs, peptide binding assays, and methyltransferase assays show that R55A/R84A specifically disrupt RNA binding while F43A specifically disrupts H3K9me3 binding, with neither affecting enzymatic activity.

results.result: RNA inhibits SUV39H1 methyltransferase activity in vitro, similar to effects observed with PRC2 and other SET domain methyltransferases.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 is supported by methyltransferase assay data showing reduced activity in the presence of RNA, consistent with cited literature on other histone methyltransferases. However, the manuscript notes this inhibition is independent of direct RNA binding based on mutant analysis.

results.result: SUV39H1 associates with α-satellite RNA in cells. RNA immunoprecipitation shows 13-fold enrichment of α-satellite RNA with WT SUV39H1 compared to GFP control, and the R55A mutation reduces this association to 45% of WT levels without disrupting HP1α binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 demonstrate SUV39H1-RNA association in cells through colocalization microscopy and RNA-IP experiments. The reduction in α-satellite RNA binding by the R55A mutant (C37) without affecting HP1α association (C38) supports direct RNA binding by SUV39H1 rather than indirect association through HP1α.

results.result: Both nucleic acid binding and H3K9me3 binding contribute to SUV39H1 localization at pericentric heterochromatin. Nucleic acid binding mutants (R55A, R84A) reduce localization to ~42-45% of WT, while aromatic cage mutants (W64A, F43A) reduce it to ~10-15% of WT. RNase treatment phenocopies the R55A mutant effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 demonstrate the relative contributions of RNA and H3K9me3 binding to SUV39H1 localization through quantitative microscopy of mutants and RNase-treated cells. The intermediate phenotype of nucleic acid binding mutants compared to aromatic cage mutants, and the equivalence of RNase treatment to the R55A mutant phenotype, support a model where both interactions are required for proper localization.

results.result: HP1α localization at heterochromatin depends on SUV39H1 and is sensitive to RNase treatment. Exogenous SUV39H1 expression increases HP1α localization 1.5-fold without changing H3K9me3 levels, and this increase is abolished by RNase treatment. HP1α localization correlates with SUV39H1 mutant localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 demonstrate that HP1α localization depends on SUV39H1 through experiments showing RNase sensitivity, correlation with SUV39H1 levels, and correlation with SUV39H1 mutant localization. The observation that SUV39H1 can recruit HP1α independently of H3K9me3 changes (C47) is particularly important for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: Nucleic acid binding stabilizes SUV39H1 association with chromatin in interphase cells. FRAP experiments show WT SUV39H1 has a recovery half-time of 27±7s with 58% mobile fraction. Nucleic acid binding mutants (R55A, R84A) show intermediate recovery (13-14s, 77% mobile), while aromatic cage mutants (W64A, F43A) show rapid recovery (5-6s, 90-95% mobile).
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C58 demonstrate the contribution of nucleic acid binding to chromatin association through FRAP analysis. The intermediate kinetics of nucleic acid binding mutants between WT and aromatic cage mutants support a model where both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding contribute to stable chromatin association. The data are internally consistent and well-quantified.

results.result: RNA Pol I inhibition with CX-5461 decreases WT SUV39H1 recovery half-time from 27±7s to 16±3s, comparable to the R55A mutant, supporting a role for nascent RNA in stabilizing SUV39H1 on chromatin.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is supported by FRAP experiments with RNA polymerase inhibitors. The similarity between CX-5461 treatment and the R55A mutant phenotype supports the conclusion that RNA transcription contributes to SUV39H1 chromatin association. However, the authors note some non-specific effects of polymerase inhibition.

results.result: Both nucleic acid binding and H3K9me3 binding by SUV39H1 are required for heterochromatin silencing. Endogenous SUV39H1 mutants (R55A, F43A, R55A/F43A) show reduced H3K9me3 levels and increased α-satellite RNA expression (1.35-2.10 fold). The R55A/F43A double mutant shows higher α-satellite RNA than F43A alone despite similar H3K9me3 levels, suggesting H3K9me3-independent contributions of RNA binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 demonstrate functional consequences of disrupting SUV39H1 binding activities using endogenous mutant cell lines. The data from western blots, immunofluorescence, and RT-qPCR show that both binding activities contribute to H3K9me3 maintenance and heterochromatin silencing. The comparison between F43A and R55A/F43A mutants (C65-C66) provides evidence for H3K9me3-independent functions of RNA binding.

results.result: The authors propose a model where chromatin-associated RNA contributes to SUV39H1 localization at constitutive heterochromatin through direct, sequence-independent binding, and that both RNA binding and H3K9me3 binding are required for proper heterochromatin function.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 represent the overall conclusions and proposed model of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the collective evidence from RNA localization, in vitro binding studies, mutant analysis, localization experiments, FRAP studies, and functional assays presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The manuscript establishes context through established knowledge about SUV39 enzymes, H3K9 methylation, heterochromatin function, and prior work on RNA-dependent chromatin regulation. This includes the role of SUV39 in catalyzing H3K9me2/3, HP1 binding to methylated histones, heterochromatin function in genome stability, and RNA-dependent mechanisms in other systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C88 represent background knowledge and prior work that contextualizes the current study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature and represent well-established findings in the field. The RNA-dependent mechanism in both human and mouse cells (C88) is supported by recent concurrent studies.
